en: Homage to the Blessed Noble Mahāpratisarā!
O wise ones, come to hear this peerless treasury of the True Dharma, which is supreme in accomplishing the welfare of the world and variegated with many jewels.
May the hosts of Rākṣasas, Mahoragas, and Daityas, as well as Garuḍas and lords of men, come here, intent upon the performance of worship. // 1 //
This noble Pratisarā, whose mere recollection is a refuge,
who is skilled in providing protection for the world on all sides,
and who has been extolled with hundreds of praises by those Tathāgatas—
I bow again to the collection that accomplishes all aims. // 2 //

[1] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the gabled hall on the peak of the Great Vajra Meru, established upon the ground of the Great Vajra Samādhi, adorned with the Great Vajra Kalpa-tree, illuminated by the radiance of precious lotuses in the Great Vajra pond, and with its floor strewn with Great Vajra sand.
In the empowerment of the great vajra, within the expanse of the great vajra-maṇḍala,
in the abode of Śakra, the lord of the gods,

adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great vajra-lion thrones, empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas through the miracle of teaching the Dharma, entering into the equality of all phenomena, and leading to omniscience.
[2] Together with eighty-four hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta-śatasahasra* of bodhisattvas, all of whom were bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*),

non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) from unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksambodhi*), who had attained great power (*mahāsthāmaprāpta*), and who displayed the miraculous transformations (*prātihārya*) of the Buddha-fields through the *mahāvajravimokṣa-samādhi*; who were endowed with the miraculous power of eloquence (*pratibhāna-prātihārya*) for teaching the Dharma— wondrous, sweet, sublime, and profound— in accordance with the mental conduct of all sentient beings in a single moment, instant, or brief interval.

[They were] with mental continuums that were solitary, purified, and cleansed by the mastery of dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and supernormal knowledges; by the doors of liberation consisting of clouds of great offerings and worship to the Tathāgatas in manifold buddha-fields; and by the unique qualities of a Buddha, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the stages, the perfections, skill in means, the articles of attraction, and the powers of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—namely, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajragarbha, and Vajragātra.

And together with Rodasī— thus indeed was the Blessed One, who had well set in motion the wheel of Dharma, who had perfectly completed the work of a Buddha, whose equipment of merit and wisdom was fully perfected,
who had attained the stage of the perfection of great awakening and omniscience which is well embraced, and whose body was adorned with the blazing marks of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

The beauty of all his limbs and members was adorned with the eighty minor marks; his crown was invisible to all beings; he had conquered all the activities of Māra; he was skilled in all the deeds of Māra; he possessed the five kinds of eyes of knowledge for all beings; he was endowed with the omniscient wisdom possessing the excellence of all aspects;
he was possessed of all the qualities of a Buddha; he was the subduer of all Māras and adversaries; and his fame, renown, and verses of praise resounded far and wide.

He who has uttered the roar of the bull and the lion, whose darkness of ignorance has been utterly severed, who has attained the perfections (*pāramitā*) of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom, skillful means, power, aspiration, and knowledge over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable and immeasurable eons;
who has never turned back from his practice of austerities; whose body is adorned with the beauty of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics;
[seated] upon a lion throne within a great vajra-jewel-lotus-womb, resounding with the tinkling of many nets of vajras, jewels, pearls, and bells.
It was firmly established upon many pedestals and footstools made of vajra-jewels; its cornices were bound with strings of red pearls disgorged from the mouths of many makaras made of vajra-jewels;
it was illuminated by the blazing rays of karketana, indranīla, mahānīla, and puṣparāga gems set within the pericarps of many lotuses made of vajra-jewels;
it was universally pleasing to behold; and it was surrounded by a protective shade formed by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of raised parasols adorned with many wands of vajra-jewels.

Seated upon a vajra-jewel lotus throne as vast as Mount Sumeru and adorned with many wish-fulfilling trees, he blazed with splendor like the king of golden mountains; the ground was resplendent with a halo of light exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like the full moon, he was lovely for all the world to behold; like a great kalpa-tree, he was in full bloom with the flowers of the Buddha-dharma.
He taught the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; he revealed the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine.
Then, from the circle of hair (*ūrṇākośa*) between his eyebrows on the crown of his head, the Blessed One emitted a web of light rays named "Manifestation of All Buddhas."
And by that network of light rays, this great trichiliocosm world-system was illuminated and made manifest.
Furthermore, all those buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, were filled with that radiance.
And in those buddha-fields, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were teaching the Dharma from within various palatial mansions and peaked towers adorned with many lion thrones.

They were teaching together with the great śrāvakas, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Then, the Blessed One addressed the vast assembly:
[13] Out of compassion for all sentient beings, I shall proclaim the *Pratisarā*;
this is a dhāraṇī that crushes all evil deeds and subdues all malevolent ones. // 1 //
By the mere hearing of which sins go to destruction;
for this [mantra] bestows happiness upon all sentient beings and liberates from all diseases. (2)
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, it was spoken by the Lord of the World for the protection of all embodied beings who are headed for miserable rebirths. (3)
Having performed protection with this [mantra], one may enter the abode of the Asuras;
likewise, one may go to Aḍakavatī, the dwelling of the Rākṣasas on earth.
In a battle terrifying and fierce with spirits, nāgas, and piśācas,
he is invincible to all enemies and even to all hosts of beings.
All planetary spirits are destroyed by the recitation and chanting of their names,
as are Skanda-demons, those possessed by madness, epilepsy, Piśācas, and likewise Ḍākinīs.
Those of great splendor who subsist on vital energy (*ojas*) indeed harm the human race; yet they are all paralyzed by the very power of the *Pratisara* mantra. (7)
Enemy armies are destroyed, as are those terrible *kākhordas*;
they are not harmed by mantra-practices, and one is liberated from root-rites (*mūlakarma*).
Neither poison, nor *gara*, nor fire, nor weapon, nor even water;
neither thunderbolt nor lightning, nor the wind of time, can cause him harm. (9)
By the splendor of this Queen of Vidyās, she crushes all enemies;
all his aims are accomplished, and he attains victory constantly. (10)
Whoever should wear this vidyā on the neck or even tied upon the arm, all their undertakings will be accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter. // 11 //
The lords of gods constantly protect them, as do the kings of the nāgas, the bodhisattvas of great heroism, the Buddhas, and the Pratyekabuddha leaders. 12.
The disciples of all the Buddhas and the goddesses of knowledge possessed of great supernatural power constantly provide protection for the one who indeed upholds the Pratisarā. (13)
Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas, and likewise the four kings will provide protection for him day and night; of this there is no doubt. (14)
And Śakra together with the thirty gods, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Nandikeśa, Mahākāla, Kārttikeya, and Gaṇeśvara.
All the hosts of Mothers, as well as others belonging to the retinue of Māra, and the sages of great splendor and the gods of great supernatural power [were there]. (16)
The Buddhas, the great-souled ones, and the powerful goddesses of knowledge shall indeed constantly provide protection for the wearer of the *pratisarā*. (17)
Māmakī and Bhṛkuṭī, as well as the goddess Tārā and Aṅkuśī;
Vajrasaṃkalayā, Śvetā, and likewise Mahāśvetā. (18)
Mahākālī and the messengers (dūtīs), as well as other Vajra-messengers; Supāśī, Vajrapāśī, Vajrapāṇi, and Mahābalā. (19)
Vajramālā is the great vidyā, and likewise Amṛtakuṇḍalī;
Aparājitā is the Great Goddess, and Kālakarṇī is of great power. // 20 //
Likewise, Dhanyā, Mahābhāgā, Padmakuṇḍalī, Puṣpadantī, Maṇicūḍā, Svarṇakeśī, and Piṅgalā; 21.
The goddess Mahātejā, as well as Dhanyā and Vidyunmālinī, the rākṣasī Ekajaṭā, and Kṣitikanāyakā—all these have awakened. // 22 //
The illustrious Kāpālinī, Dhanyā, and likewise Laṅkeśvarī, as well as many other vidyās that bring benefit to sentient beings. (23)
Hārītī, Pāñcika, Śaṅkhinī, and Kūṭadantinī will provide protection for that person in whose hand this vidyā resides. (24)
The goddess Śrī and Sarasvatī themselves, as constant followers, always protect that woman who constantly wears this Mahāpratisarā. (25)
All success shall belong to her, and she shall always have sons in her womb;
the fetuses grow in comfort, and the pregnant woman gives birth in comfort. (26)
Diseases are destroyed and all evils perish, of this there is no doubt;
he becomes meritorious and strong, and constantly increases in wealth and grain. (27)
Furthermore, whoever—whether a woman or even a man—purely maintains this, shall have speech that is authoritative and shall become worthy of honor. (28)
He shall be intent upon the liberation of all sentient beings, and he shall always be happy, free from all diseases. (29)
Kings, along with their harems and great retinues, come under his influence;
he constantly blazes with splendor, and his mass of merit increases.
All ritual manuals are accomplished for one who has entered all mandalas; such a person, knowing the commitments everywhere, acts according to the word of the Victor. // 31 //
Bad dreams do not afflict one; it is supreme in removing all sins.
Evils are destroyed, and likewise, adversaries as well. 32.
This was spoken by the Great Lords of Knowledge for the purpose of destroying all seizing spirits;
indeed, it grants all desires for whoever meditates upon it constantly. (33)
I shall now proclaim this; O hosts of spirits, listen to me!

This is the Aparājitā Dhāraṇī, whose heart is the Cintāmaṇi mudrā vibrating with the purity of a universal garland of flames; it belongs to this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Vidyās.
O Great Brāhmaṇa, by the mere hearing of it, that son of good family or daughter of good family becomes completely liberated from all evil.
Furthermore, O Great Brāhmaṇa, he in whom this dwells in the heart should be known as one who possesses a vajra-body.
Fire shall not pass through his body.
Why is this known?
When the prince Rāhulabhadra was in the womb of his mother in the great and excellent city of Kapilavastu, the Śākya maiden Gopā threw herself into a pit of fire.
Thereupon a lotus pond appeared.
At that time, while Prince Rāhulabhadra was still within the womb, he brought this vidyā to mind;
by the mere recollection of this vidyā, that fire became cool at that very moment.
Then, the body of Gopā, the Śākya maiden, was not touched by fire.
For what reason?
Because this spell is empowered by the empowerment of all the Tathāgatas.
For that reason, O Great Brāhmaṇa, fire does not burn him,
nor can he be deprived of life by poison.
How is this so?

[18] O Great Brāhmaṇa, when the son of the merchant Kośabalika—who was a master of spells—lived in the great and excellent city of Śūrpāraka, he used the power of his spells to summon Takṣaka, the king of the nāgas.
Having summoned him, however, because of negligence, he bound him but did not subdue him. Eventually, he was bitten by him out of anger, and he experienced intense pain.
And he knew that my life had ceased.
There, many magicians were summoned, yet not one was able to counteract the poison.
Now, in that very great city of Śūrpāraka, there lived a laywoman named Vimalaśuddhi, who was endowed with great compassion.
This Great Queen of Spells appeared before her face.
She approached her, and having approached, she set this Great Spell in motion.

By merely recollecting it once, she rendered [the poison] non-toxic, restored her memory, and having liberated her from that great calamity, she caused this very Great Spell to dwell within her heart.
"As it was duly authorized.
Furthermore, Great Brāhmaṇa, what has been fully understood?
As he wandered gradually through the great city of Vārāṇasī, he came to be known as King Brahmadatta.

"What means indeed might we employ by which this enemy army could be destroyed?
Give us your command.
The king said:
"Be of little concern, sirs!

"What is this, Great King?

"I shall now perform a direct vision. Then King Brahmadatta, having bathed his head with various scented waters, having put on pure garments, and having written down this Great King of Vidyās according to the ritual procedure and placed it within a head-case, and having donned this very armor of the Queen of Vidyās, [stood] in the midst of the battle.
"Having descended alone, this entire fourfold army was defeated;
and having been crushed by her, that King of the Wheel of Power (Balacakrarāja) went for refuge and was released.

Therefore, O Great Brāhmaṇa, you should hold it in mind that this Queen of Great Spells (Mahāvidyārājñī), whose great majesty is directly perceptible, is empowered by the heart-seals (hṛdayamudrā) of all the Tathāgatas and is indeed manifest."
This should be regarded as equal to all the Tathāgatas.
In the future time, in the final age, it should be regarded as being for the benefit of those beings who have short lifespans, meager merit, and limited fortune.
O Great Brāhmaṇa, whoever shall write down this Mahāpratisarā, the Queen of Great Vidyās, according to the rite, and wear it on their arm or neck, should be known as empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
It should be known as the body of all Tathāgatas;
it should be known as the vajra-body;
it should be known as the womb containing the essence of all Tathāgatas.
He should be known as the Eye of all Tathāgatas;
he should be known as the Body of Blazing Radiance;
he should be known as the Impenetrable Armor.
It should be known as the crusher of all enemies;
it should be known as the burner away of all sinful obscurations;
it should be known as the purifier of the hellish realm of rebirth.
"What was it, Great Brāhmaṇa, that you previously understood?

In a certain place, there was a monk who lacked faith, who violated the lineage and training of the Tathāgata, and who took what was not given. He would steal the keys to the gateways of pleasure and, having appropriated for himself all the property belonging to the Saṅgha, to the four quarters, or to the community, he consumed it as his own private possession."
Then, at another time, he was afflicted by a great illness and experienced intense, agonizing pain.
That ascetic, being without protection and without refuge, let out a great cry of lamentation.
Now, in that very same place, there lived a brahmin lay follower.
He heard that sound;
having heard it, he approached where that monk was, and upon arriving, he wrote down this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, and tied it around the monk’s neck.
As soon as the Great Amulet was tied on, all of that monk’s pains were pacified, he was completely freed from all diseases, and he became restored to health.
At the end of that very night, with his mindfulness well-established, he passed away;
once his body had been cast off, he was reborn in the great Avīci hell.
And his dead body was placed upon a funeral pyre by the monks.
That Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, remained fastened around his neck.
Immediately upon that monk’s rebirth there, all the painful sensations of those beings in the Avīci hell were pacified,
and those beings in the hells became endowed with every happiness.
"And even those great masses of fire of the Avīci hell have all been completely extinguished.
Then those messengers of Yama, trembling, reported this decision of Yama, the King of Dharma, in detail:

The terrible sufferings of sentient beings, which are born of their karma, have been pacified. // 1 //
Even those embers situated within the bodies of embodied beings are always stilled;
the saw-teeth do not cause affliction, and the razor-edge does not adhere.
All weapons are shattered and the iron jars are stilled;
furthermore, the leaves born of karma no longer cause affliction in the Forest of Sword-Leaves.
"You are Yama, the King of Dharma, and you govern men according to righteousness.

Then that righteous king, whose very soul was dharma and who was firm in the principles of dharma, having heard such words from those who were lost in their hearts of compassion, [spoke as follows]. (5)
"Tell me quickly, what is this? How is it so? Then those extremely fierce servants of Yama spoke to those wicked beings.
They spoke these words to Yama, the King of Dharma:

Because his name is "Avīci," he is called Saṃkaṭa;
he by whom the diversity of karmas exists, and by whom sentient beings have been made happy.
For this person is happy everywhere and shall go again to the abode of the gods;
even Yama, the King of Dharma, having seen him, speaks in amazement. (9)
This one possesses great supernatural power, and his body from previous births is vast;
just as the stupa of the Teacher shines with hundreds of collections of relics. (10)
In this way his body shines, with the *pratisarā* amulet bound around his neck.
Then those *yakṣa* guardians of hell spoke these words to Yama, the King of Dharma: "O Lord, why is this called a *pratisarā*?"
The King of Dharma said:
He who causes one to remember the *Pratipad* does not go to a miserable rebirth;
for he, being permeated by the essence of the *Pratisarā*, goes to a happy rebirth.
Alternatively, O guardians of hell, go indeed to Puṣkalāvatī;
there you shall see Mahākūṭa surrounded by deities. (12)
"Having seen that, you shall develop a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.

they then saw him there, near the royal capital.

indeed, those yakṣas established for him a place named Pratisarakūṭa.
Then those yakṣas, having returned once more, reported in detail to Yama, the King of Dharma, his decision.

Consequently, this must certainly be upheld, recited, and written; it should always be worn upon the body according to the prescribed rite.

One crosses over from all fears and terrors of miserable rebirths, and it is not possible for lightning to strike them.

[26] O Great Brahmin, in the excellent great city of Hiṅgumardana, there was a merchant named Vimalaśaṅkha, who was immensely wealthy with vast gold, possessed of full treasuries and granaries,
and renowned as a caravan leader (sārthavāha). Then that great caravan leader, having obtained a ship, set out upon the great ocean.
Meanwhile, that ship was seized by *timiṅgila* fish;
and the *nāgas*, desiring to destroy it, became agitated and made a great roar and crashing sound, emitting lightning-bolts and beginning to rain down thunderbolts.
Then those merchants, their minds struck by great suffering, [beheld] that great agitation of the *nāgas* and the lightning-bolts.
Seeing the thunderbolt being hurled and the ship seized by those *timiṅgila* fish, they began to raise a great cry of lamentation;
they supplicated various deities,
yet not one of them provided them protection.
Then, approaching the caravan leader, they spoke these words most piteously:
"Save us, O Great Being! Deliver us from this great terror!
Thereupon, the great caravan leader, firm-minded and of great intelligence— // 1 //
To the merchants who had become distraught, he spoke these words:
"Do not fear, do not fear, O merchants; attain steadfastness."
"I shall deliver you from this great ocean of suffering.
Then, becoming firm of mind, the merchants spoke these words: (3)
"Tell us quickly and without hindrance, O Great Being:
as long as we live, O Great-minded One, it shall be through your power. (4)
"Tell us the greatness of this knowledge; what will you do afterwards?
Thereupon, the caravan leader recited this spell for them.
I possess a great vidyā known as Pratisarā,
which subdues all malevolent beings and possesses great power and prowess.
"Therefore, I shall liberate you from this great fear of extreme suffering.
Then, at that very moment, that great caravan leader had this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, written down and hoisted upon the top of a banner.
As soon as this Great Amulet was hoisted upon the banner-top, all those *timiṅgila* fish saw that boat as if it were a single mass of blazing fire.
Then those nāgas, with minds full of loving-kindness, descended into their presence and began to offer worship.

And those *timiṅgila* fish, being scorched by the power of this very *Mahāpratisarā-vidyārājñī*, fled away and were destroyed; and those merchants were brought by those great nāgas to a vast island of great jewels.
[28] This Great Knowledge, Mahāpratisarā, is empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
For that reason, O Great Brāhmaṇa, it is known as "Great Knowledge.
It must certainly be worn after having been placed at the top of a banner.
It pacifies all winds, cold, untimely clouds, lightning, and thunderbolts;
it brings about complete liberation from all conflicts and disputes among gods, humans, and non-humans;
and various kinds of creatures such as gadflies, mosquitoes, locusts, and other species that destroy crops have no power over it.
They attain tranquility;
all wicked-minded beasts, birds, and fanged creatures perish;
and all flowers, fruits, leaves, trees, medicinal herbs, crops, and so forth, flourish abundantly.
They will be savory, sweet, and soft;
they will be perfectly ripened.
All the evils of excessive rain and drought will cease to exist in every respect.
There will be rain in due season, not out of season;

and those great nāgas in that region will release showers of rain correctly and at the proper times. In whatever region this Great Queen of Spells named Mahāpratisarā shall circulate, there by those beings—
Having understood this, one should perform worship and honor with various perfumes, incenses, flowers, and garments;
having wrapped [the image] and fixed a banner atop a stūpa, one should circumambulate it while various musical instruments and songs are being played.
For those great beings, the deities beginning with Śakra and Brahmā will fulfill their hopes exactly as they have conceived them.
Alternatively, in whatever manner it is written according to the prescribed rite, in that very way it prospers:
one desiring a son obtains a son, and another woman who is carrying a fetus will carry it with ease; the fetus develops comfortably, and she gives birth with ease. // 1 //
"In time the fetus grows, and in time it is released. Why is this so? O Great Brāhmaṇa, listen as before:
here in the very realm of Magadha, there was a king named Prasāritapāṇi."
And he remained childless.
Why was he known as "Extended-Hand"?
Because as soon as he was born, the king extended his hand, took hold of his mother’s breast, and drank as much milk as he desired.

And those two breasts, by the mere touch [of his hand], became the color of gold; and they constantly increased with a great flow of milk. For that reason, the name "Prasāritapāṇi" (Outstretched Hand) was established for the king.

Furthermore, whenever supplicants came to that king, the king would extend his right hand into the air. Because he was a Bodhisattva, the deities who were devoted to the Buddha filled his hand with divine, exquisite jewels and gold gems;
the king then bestowed these upon those people who had come as supplicants.
By the mere thought of it, he gave to all supplicants whatever they desired for their happiness and prosperity;
and for the sake of a son, he performed great acts of worship and honor toward the gods, yet he did not obtain a son.
He then began to repeatedly pay homage to the ancient stūpas of the Tathāgatas.
He performs great acts of worship and honor,
gives gifts,
and observes the fast.
He performs great meritorious deeds;
he gives gifts that are truly inexhaustible.
For what reason?

[30] Once upon a time, O Great Brahmin, in this very land of Magadha, in the country of the Mallas, in the great and excellent city of Kuśinagara, there lived under the teaching of the Blessed One Prabhūtaratna a certain great being, a merchant named Dharmamati, who was devoted to the Dharma and possessed a mind set on the Dharma.
Having established a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings, he taught the Dharma beginning with this very Great Knowledge, the Mahāpratisarā.
Then, a certain poor man, having heard that Dharma, spoke these words to the great merchant:
"I shall perform labor as a hired servant in the noble one's residence, and I shall listen to the Dharma."
"When I have something [to offer], then I shall honor the Dharma.
While he was thus occupied with his household affairs and listening to the Dharma, at another time that merchant gave him a single *dīnāra*.

Having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) for the sake of protecting all sentient beings, and having made it common to all beings, he offered it as the Great Amulet Jewel (*Mahāpratisarāratna*).
And thus a vow was made:
"By this great fruit of giving, may there be the complete eradication of poverty for myself and for all sentient beings.
For that reason, that gift does not go to exhaustion.

[31] Having thus performed such manifold and diverse accumulations of merit and having worshipped as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there were, the deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm then granted him a vision in a dream and spoke as follows:
"O Great King, this is the Mahāpratisarā, the Queen of Vidyās, the great dhāraṇī named Aparājitā, whose heart is the Cintāmaṇi seal vibrating with the purity of a garland of universal flames."

"Having drawn [the diagram] according to the ritual, and having fasted according to the ritual as prescribed in the manual, once you have bound it to the body of the chief queen, the goddess, according to the ritual, then you will obtain a son. Then, when that night had passed, the king woke up; he assembled a group of brahmins skilled in calculation, writing, constellations, planets, and the five-fold analysis, and according to the ritual, when the Puṣya constellation—the king of constellations—had arrived, she bathed her limbs thoroughly.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rite, the chief queen, the goddess, had this Mahāpratisarā, the Queen of Vidyās, inscribed and bound around her neck;
she performed great worship at the great Buddhist stūpas and bestowed many excellent jewels as gifts for sentient beings.
Then, after the lapse of nine months, a son was born, handsome, pleasing, and beautiful, endowed with the most excellent and abundant splendor of complexion.

Knowing this, O Great Brāhmaṇa, there is the Queen of Great Spells (Mahāvidyārājñī), renowned as the Mahāpratisarā-ratna, who fulfills all desires, is unconquerable, and is worshipped by all the Tathāgatas.
This crest-jewel belongs to Śakra in every respect.

Whenever Śakra, the lord of the gods, desires to engage in a great battle with the asuras, he then puts on this very armor, places it upon his crest, and having conquered and defeated all the asuras, enters the city of the gods in happiness, well-being, and safety.
He becomes unassailable by all asuras.

For in this way, O Great Brahmin, for a bodhisattva who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, maintains this Mahāpratisarā, the Great Queen of Vidyās, there is invincibility against all Māras;
whoever shall have this residing in their body or throat will be empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
He will be protected by all bodhisattvas;
he will be constantly and perpetually saluted, honored, and revered by all gods, humans, kings, royal ministers, brahmins, and householders;
and he will be worshipped and venerated by all gods, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
"He is a Mahāsattva," said the Blessed One, the crusher of Māra’s forces.
"He shall be free from all diseases,
and all his calamities and misfortunes shall be pacified."
That Great Being will be free from all sorrow,
and all the deities will constantly and continuously provide him with protection, defense, and guardianship.
Furthermore, he should constantly and continuously write down these four great heart-mantras of Aparājita and carry them upon his person.
Having performed them, they should be maintained, constantly and continuously brought to mind, recited, and cultivated with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).
All evil dreams, ill omens, and inauspicious states will perish, and all forms of happiness and prosperity will manifest.
Herein, these mantra-words are perfected, auspicious, and effective for all rites.
Oṃ amṛtavare vara vara pravaraviśuddhe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā / Oṃ amṛtavilokini garbhasaṃrakṣaṇi ākarṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā / This is the Heart Mantra of Aparājitā.

[36] All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas without exception, having assembled together in one place, spoke these mantra-words of the dhāraṇī with a single resonance:
"These mantra-words—the heart and armor of the Great Amulet, the Great Queen of Vidyās—are sealed with the seal of all the Tathāgatas.
Even to hear them is exceedingly rare; how much more so to write, recite, read, retain, and explain them to others!"
It should be understood that this is the work of a Buddha;
for this great dhāraṇī is exceedingly praised, rejoiced in, and prophesied by all the Tathāgatas, and it is most difficult to encounter.

The Aparājitā Mahāpratisarā— whose very name is extremely difficult to obtain— is the destroyer of all evil, possessed of great strength and prowess, great majesty, and great power; she reveals great virtues, destroys all the deities belonging to the hosts of Māra, and severs the fetters of Māra that consist of the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

This great dhāraṇī is the destroyer of those with malicious intent who employ supreme mantras, mudrās, poisons, kākhordas, powders, and the casting of rays, as well as practices of incantation, hatred, and malevolent magic.
It is the protector of those who delight in making offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the excellent assembly of noble ones.
This great dhāraṇī is the guardian of those devoted to the Mahāyāna through its reception, writing, reciting, reading, chanting, hearing, and upholding.
O Great Brahmā, as long as it brings to fulfillment the awakening of a Buddha, this Mahāpratisarā Queen of Vidyās is not obstructed anywhere;

and everywhere she receives great worship, just as I, the Teacher who has conquered all enemies, do. Why is this? Because this great vidyā was previously known to be the destroyer of all obstacles and impediments.

And when the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipulaprahasitavadanamaṇikanakaratnojjvalaraśmiprabhāsābhyudgatarāja, having first attained perfect awakening, approached the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) desiring to turn the wheel of Dharma praised by all Buddhas, at that time, for that Blessed One, by all the Māras—

Accompanied by their retinues and surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Māras— filled with various forms, misshapen and terrifying sounds, and empowered by the manifold transformations of the realm of Māra— they arrived, conjuring a rain of various weapons, and having encircled the four directions, more than hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of limitless and boundless Evil Ones began to create obstacles.

Then the Blessed One, King of the Emergence of Radiant Light from Jewels, Gold, and Gems, Whose Face is Widely Smiling, remained silent for a moment and mentally recited this Great Amulet, the Great Vidyā, seven times. As soon as this Great Amulet, the King of Vidyās, was recited, at that very instant all those Māras...

The evil ones saw emerging from each single pore of the Blessed One hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings, clad in armor and bound with mail, holding flaming swords, axes, nooses, mallets, clubs, and tridents in their hands, uttering these words:
"Seize! Bind! Destroy the wicked Māras! Crush the lives of those with evil minds! Annihilate all wicked grahas, obstacles, and vināyakas who seek to harm the Blessed One!"

Then, having completely conquered all those wicked Māras with the sword of loving-kindness (*maitrī-khaḍga*), some were made to take up the precepts (*śikṣāpada*), while others were even prophesied (*vyākṛta*) for unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); such was the great majesty [of the Buddha].

Furthermore, when other [Māras] saw those Great Beings (*mahāpuruṣa*) emerging from the pores of the Tathāgata’s skin, they became utterly distraught in that city; deprived of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), their eloquence, strength, and prowess destroyed, they were utterly shattered.
"Thinking that they had all fled,
the Blessed One then set in motion the Wheel of Dharma just as other Buddhas have done;
having utterly destroyed all obstacles, impediments, and the Evil Māras, he has crossed over and reached the further shore."
[38] For in this way, O Great Brahmā, this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, who has attained the perfection of supernatural power with great strength and speed,
liberates from all calamities, fears, and terrors by mere recollection those beings whose intentions are pure,
but not others whose minds are wicked.
Therefore, O Great Brahmin, it should always be attended to through constant recollection and mental engagement;
and at all times, having written it down and placed it upon the body, it should be maintained.
Why? Because it is as previously stated in the words.
In the great city of Ujjayinī, within the realm of King Brahmadatta, a certain man committed an offense.
He was ordered by King Brahmadatta to the executioners:
"Sirs, go and deprive this man of his life."
Then those executioners, having seized that man who had been commanded by the king, went to a mountain cave; drawing their swords from their scabbards, they began to deprive that man of his life.
At that time, that man mentally recollected this Mahāpratisarā, the Queen of Great Spells, and he wore it written upon his right arm.
By the power of this Great Being and this great spell, the sword became a single flame and was shattered into pieces like scattered dust.
Then those executioners reported this very matter in detail to the king.
Thereupon, the king, becoming enraged, said:
"Go, men! In a certain region there is a yakṣa cave where many hundreds of thousands of flesh-eating yakṣas dwell. Take him there and abandon him."
Then that man was cast into that yakṣa cave by those executioners.

As soon as he had been cast into the yakṣa cave, all those yakṣas ran forward with joyful minds, thinking, "We shall devour this human being! But through the power of this Mahāpratisarā, they saw that man.
Seeing him blazing intensely with a garland of single-flamed rays, everyone became terrified and perceived their own bodies as being consumed by fire.
Then those yakṣas were struck with wonder; they seized that man, placed him outside the gate, and began to circumambulate him.
Meanwhile, those executioners reported to the king in detail what his resolve had been.
Then the king, becoming even more enraged and fierce, said:
"If it is so, sirs, go, bind this man and throw him into the river!
He was bound by those men and thrown into the river.

and those bonds were shattered into pieces. This was heard by the king.
Then the king, his face blossoming with wonder, said:
"Aha! What a marvel this man is!
It is my reflection that there must be some cause for this."
Then that king, having summoned that man, spoke thus:
"Do you know, O man?
The man replied:
"Great King, I do not know anything at all, except that I maintain the Great Amulet, the Great Vidyā-mantra.
It is solely through its power, O Lord.
The King said:
Oh, what a great marvel!
This great vidyā has been well-spoken;
it deludes the rod of death and is empowered by all the Buddhas.
She is the savior of all sentient beings, the liberator from sickness and suffering. // 1 //
This great vidyā of great splendor, which liberates from untimely death and wards off great diseases, has been spoken by the compassionate Lords. (2)

[41] Thus, O Great Brahmin, this Great Amulet, the Queen of Spells, receives great honor everywhere.
She is not to be transgressed by any beings with malicious minds.
This Queen of Great Vidyās has been fully understood from of old; she is never thwarted anywhere.
Therefore, it must certainly be worn, having been placed upon the body.
"Furthermore, Great Brahmin, this should be written by Sunakṣatra according to the most excellent ritual procedure.
